bib.title: Text Analytics with Python, Chapter 2: Python Refresher

question: What Python language features, setup steps and text-handling tools does a reader need before doing text analytics?
contributions: Refresher of Python setup, syntax, data types, control flow, functional constructs, classes, string handling, regexes and text analytics libraries.

results.claim: The chapter says Python 3 makes all text strings Unicode by default, unlike Python 2.
results.setup: Python 2.x vs 3.x string handling; the book uses Python 2.7.11
results.quote: By default, all strings are Unicode in  Python 3.x , but they are not

results.claim: In Python 2, the regex \w+ does not match an accented letter in a Unicode string unless re.UNICODE is passed, so 'Hello' with an accent splits into two tokens.
results.quote: need to explicitly specify the unicode flag to detect it using regex

results.quote: They often work very well on streaming data where you cannot keep

limits: Python 2.7.11 code (print statements, .next(), u'' literals); dated, Python 2 reached end of life in 2020.
No experiments; performance claims (comprehensions faster than loops, PyPy 10x-100x, 100 lines reduced to 20) are asserted without data.
Regex \w behaviour shown is Python 2; in Python 3 str patterns are Unicode-aware by default.
practices: Use virtual environments so projects with conflicting library versions can coexist (Virtual Environments, p. 64).
Prefer conda over pip on Windows for packages like numpy and scipy (Environment Setup, p. 64).
Use raw strings r'...' for regex patterns and Windows paths to avoid escape interpretation (String Literals, p. 95).
Use dict.get instead of indexing to avoid KeyError (Dictionaries, p. 76).
Use generators for large or streaming data so it need not be held in memory (Generators, p. 90).
Be aware that Python 2 strings are not Unicode by default when handling text (Working with Text, p. 94).
